Humboldt squid Dosidicus gigas exhibits a life history strategy finely tuned to the dynamic environment of the eastern Pacific. Field-based studies indicate that juveniles begin life as minuscule, free-swimming paralarvae weighing only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] at the onset of exogenous feeding, a value derived from direct measurements of hatchlings emerging from egg masses with a mean diameter of 1 millimeter. The duration of the embryonic period is strongly temperature-dependent, with paralarvae hatching after just 6 days [ab = 6 days] when incubated at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a developmental pace characteristic of ommastrephid squids in warm-water regions. In contrast, under cooler conditions typical of the species' northern range, this incubation period can extend substantially. Upon hatching, these minute paralarvae immediately commence a planktotrophic feeding mode, preying on copepods and other small zooplankton to fuel their rapid somatic growth.

Sexual maturation in Dosidicus gigas is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age, with individuals initiating gonadal development upon reaching a mantle length of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters]. This size threshold signals the onset of puberty, which in turn triggers a fundamental shift in the squid's foraging behavior and vertical distribution patterns. Both sexes attain this developmental milestone during their first year of life, though the exact age at maturation is highly plastic and modulated by local oceanographic conditions and prey availability. The length at which puberty occurs represents a critical inflection point in the species' energetic budget, as resources previously allocated exclusively to somatic growth are now partially diverted towards gamete production and the complex behaviors associated with spawning aggregations.

A remarkable terminal investment strategy defines the reproductive output of female Humboldt squid. Based on necropsies of spent individuals collected from aggregations in the Gulf of California, a single female that has completed her reproductive lifespan carries a cumulative fecundity of approximately 20 million oocytes  in her oviducts and ovarian tissue at the time of at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C] natural death. This staggering investment was recorded at an ambient water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], typical of the deep, oxygen-minimum zone waters these squids inhabit during their spawning periods. The sheer magnitude of this reproductive output ranks among the highest documented for any cephalopod and underscores the species' semelparous, single-spawning life history, where a female expends nearly all of her available energy reserves in a single, massive spawning event before succumbing to physiological exhaustion.

Sexual dimorphism in maximum body size is pronounced in this species, with females attaining substantially larger terminal dimensions than males. Growth trajectory analyses of captured individuals show that the largest females can reach a mantle length of 120 centimeters [Li = 120 centimeters] at death, whereas their male counterparts max out at a more modest 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters] at death. This disparity in final size is accompanied by a similarly stark difference in total wet weight; an old female approaching natural death can attain a staggering 65 kilograms [Wwi = 65 kilograms] of wet mass, a figure that reflects both her larger mantle dimensions and the engorged condition of her reproductive organs. The progression from a birth weight of just 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] to this enormous terminal mass represents a weight increase of over eight orders of magnitude and necessitates a consistently high food intake throughout life.

The environmental temperature regime exerts a powerful effect on the species' overall pace of life, particularly on its maximum longevity. For female Humboldt squid, the total duration from hatching to senescent death has been estimated at approximately 730 days [am = approximately 730 days] for individuals reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a thermal condition that approximates the average temperature of their epipelagic foraging habitat. This two-year lifespan is relatively short for an animal of such large terminal body size and reflects the extraordinarily rapid growth rates enabled by a warm-water, high-metabolic lifestyle and an abundant supply of micronektonic prey. Comparative data from cooler, upwelling-influenced waters suggest that longevity may increase as metabolic rates slow, though growth rates and final body sizes tend to decrease correspondingly. An integrated understanding of these thermal dependencies remains essential for predicting how climate-driven shifts in ocean temperature will impact the population dynamics of this ecologically dominant predator.
